food.text: Sugarcane first entered Japan in the eighth century, but sugar stayed rare until sugarcane was reintroduced in the 16th century. Even then it was used sparingly and held the status of a luxury, and most consumption remained medicinal.

During the Edo period, vinegar rather than fermented rice began to be used in sushi, and haya-zushi, or "fast sushi", was developed. Simply mixing rice with vinegar eliminated the fermentation process, so sushi became a fast food. A 1689 cookbook describes haya-zushi.
The sweet potato was introduced to Okinawa in 1605. It became a staple food there and remained one until the beginning of the 20th century.

In 1609, Japan invaded the Ryukyu islands and captured the sugar industry. In the 1630s the Sakoku system left Nagasaki as the only place where trade was permitted, so sugar still reached Japan there. Much of it came from Dutch traders, who liked sugar shipments for the ballast they provided their ships.

In the first half of the 18th century, Tokugawa Yoshimune promoted domestic sugar production to reduce Japan's trade deficit, ordering that sugarcane be planted across Japan. By 1800 Japan was producing more sugar than it was importing.

Pork became important in Okinawan cooking when it diffused in the seventeenth century in response to demands from Chinese ambassadors, who preferred it to beef. Since Ryukyu was a tributary state to China, Ryukyuan cooks also traveled to Fujian Province to learn how to cook Chinese food.
The Portuguese introduced castella, a sweet, rectangular sponge cake, to Nagasaki in the 16th century. It is now popular throughout Japan.

Some places specialized in particular sugars. Okinawa and Amami Ōshima produced brown sugar, while the island of Shikoku made a fine-grained sugar that became known as wasanbon. It gained favor among the elite for its use in making wagashi.

Rice and ingredients rolled in nori appeared after the sheet form of nori seaweed was invented around 1750. The term makizushi was first used in the book Ryōri Sankaikyō in 1749, but that dish was instead seafood rolled with a bamboo mat, or makisu.

Records dating to the 18th century attest to the Early Modern Korean word 도슭, from which dosirak, the packed lunch, is derived. Unlike the more formal chanhap enjoyed by the nobility, Joseon era peasants and soldiers carried lunch in a simple woven bamboo or wood tumak box.

From the Edo period late into the Meiji era, street vendors donned costumes they thought Chinese to sell sweets. They chanted songs in a language they thought sounded Chinese, since the international sourcing of sugar lent sweets a perception of foreignness.

Current-day makizushi first appeared in the book Shinsen Kondate buruishū in 1776, which describes spreading cooked rice on a makisu and arranging fishes on it. In 1778, a food shop guide book called Shichijyūgonichi listed a shop whose most famous dish was norimaki-zushi.

art.text: Ukiyo-e prints of the world of kabuki theater and the pleasure districts began to be produced in the late 17th century. In 1765 Harunobu produced the first polychrome print. This school of art is the one best known in the West.

Two 16th-century structures show the polarities of Japanese art. The Katsura Detached Palace is an exercise in simplicity, with rough, untrimmed natural materials and beauty achieved by accident. Nikkō Tōshō-gū is rigidly symmetrical, with brightly colored relief carvings covering every visible surface.

After the first Portuguese ships arrived in Kyushu in 1543, Nanban art developed in Japan. Its folding screens, called Nanban byōbu, are especially notable, with over 90 pairs surviving today. They show foreigners arriving in Japanese ports and walking in the streets of inland towns.

The word Nanban was originally a Sino-Japanese term for the peoples of South Asia and Southeast Asia, meaning 'Southern barbarians'. During the Nanban trade period it came to designate the Portuguese, who first arrived in 1543, and later other Europeans. It also refers to paintings that Europeans brought to Japan.

Artists of the Kanō school were joined by those of the Tosa school in combining foreign subject matter with Japanese styles of painting. Foreign warriors were another popular subject. Western canons such as linear perspective appear to have had little lasting influence in Japan.

Japan was unified under Oda Nobunaga and Toyotomi Hideyoshi after a long period of civil war, and the Ōnin War had earlier led to the rise of castle architecture. The two rulers built castles as symbols of their power, Nobunaga in Azuchi and Hideyoshi in Momoyama. Each castle had a central tower called a tenshu, set within massive stone walls and deep moats. Artists decorated the dark interiors, which were divided by sliding fusuma panels and byōbu folding screens.

After the Ōnin War (1467–1477), Japan entered a century of political, social and economic turmoil. Under the Tokugawa shogunate that later emerged, organized religion played a much less important role in people's lives. The arts that survived were primarily secular.

Nanban art declined because Christianity was persecuted and prohibited in Japan from the end of the sixteenth century. The Tokugawa policy of sakoku, which largely closed Japan to foreign contact from the 1630s, sealed its fate.

The tea ceremony emphasised simplicity and modest design as a counterpoint to the excesses of the aristocracy. In the Azuchi–Momoyama period, sukiya-zukuri villas appeared under the influence of the tea house, or chashitsu. In the Edo period the style was applied to ryōtei, Japanese-style restaurants.

The generation of print designers after Harunobu included Torii Kiyonaga and Utamaro. They created elegant and sometimes insightful depictions of courtesans, part of the ukiyo-e world of the demimonde.

Japanese crafts traveled far beyond Asia in this era. The Manila Galleons sailed between Manila and Acapulco from 1565 to 1815, and the trade in Japanese crafts they carried left earlier evidence of Japanese influence in the art of Colonial Mexico.

war.text: Between 1592 and 1598, Toyotomi Hideyoshi launched two Japanese invasions of Korea, and Japan quickly occupied large portions of the country. Reinforcements from Ming China and disruption of Japanese supply fleets by the Joseon Navy forced the Japanese to withdraw from the northern provinces. The conflict ended in 1598 with the withdrawal of Japanese forces from the Korean Peninsula.

On October 26, 1597, Admiral Yi Sun-sin held the Myeongnyang Strait with only 13 ships left after a disastrous Korean defeat at Chilcheollyang, where the Japanese navy had virtually wiped out the Joseon fleet and Admiral Wŏn Kyun was killed. All sources agree the Japanese ships outnumbered the Korean ones by at least ten to one. The battle ended as a humiliating naval defeat for Japan, with many Japanese killed and many sailors drowned in the currents of the strait.

At the Battle of Nagashino in 1575, the allied forces of Oda Nobunaga and Tokugawa Ieyasu, numbering 38,000, crushed Takeda Katsuyori's 15,000 men. According to Shinchō Kōki, Takeda lost 10,000 men, two-thirds of his original besieging force, and several of the Twenty-Four Generals of Takeda Shingen were killed. The battle is often cited as the first "modern" battle in Japan, because Nobunaga defeated the Takeda cavalry with powerful arquebusiers using tanegashima.

When Toyotomi Hideyoshi's Japan invaded Korea between 1592 and 1598, the advance was halted by Korean forces. Most notable was the Joseon Navy led by Admiral Yi Sun-sin, with his renowned "turtle ship".

Takeda Katsuyori surrounded Nagashino Castle, which had only 500 defenders, with 15,000 men. Tokugawa Ieyasu could mobilise only about 8,000 troops and judged he could not stand against the Takeda army alone. He asked his ally Oda Nobunaga for support.

At Myeongnyang, 31 Japanese warships were sunk or crippled, and the commander Tōdō Takatora was wounded. Kurushima was killed and the Japanese suffered extremely heavy casualties, with a captured prisoner reporting that half were killed or wounded. Many Japanese sailors who abandoned sinking or damaged ships drowned in the strong currents, which kept them from swimming to shore. Even so, the Joseon navy was still outnumbered, so Admiral Yi withdrew to the Yellow Sea to resupply his fleet and gain more space for a mobile defense.

Because Japan had been at war since the mid-15th century, Hideyoshi could build a professional army from a pool of 500,000 battle-hardened soldiers. His 1588 "sword hunt" and 1591 "Separation Edict" showed a new unity in Japan. The edict ended wokou piracy by forbidding daimyos to support pirates.

Oda Nobunaga chose to camp at Shitaragahara because it was a depression. Taking advantage of the terrain, he positioned his 30,000-strong army so that it did not look like a large force from the Takeda side. He had left Gifu on 21 June and arrived on 26 June. When the Takeda army, with its retreat cut off, charged his positions, repeated charges were blocked by matchlock guns and horse defense fences, and with many of its troops killed it began to retreat. Nobunaga pounced on them when their ranks gave way, inflicting even more casualties.

The victory at Myeongnyang convinced the Ming government that it could ease security at its major ports and deploy a fleet to help the Joseon navy. The Chinese navy joined Admiral Yi in early 1598. Many ships and sailors who had been in hiding after Chilcheollyang also joined his fleet.

The Joseon court had initially dismissed arquebuses as useless because of their low rate of fire. They were rapidly adopted during and after the Imjin War, and domestic production began as early as 1593. Some scholars think this helped the Joseon-Ming army avoid easy defeat in 1597.

Korean forces halted Japan's invasion, most notably the Joseon Navy led by Admiral Yi Sun-sin and his renowned "turtle ship". They were helped by righteous army militias of Korean civilians and by Ming Chinese troops. The war-weakened Joseon was then invaded by the Manchus in 1627 and 1637.

Japanese swords, sometimes collected on the battlefield from dead Japanese soldiers, inspired some of the basic designs of later Korean swords such as the hwando. It was one of the technological and cultural transfers that came out of the Imjin War.

A famous legend tells that at the fourth battle of Kawanakajima, Uesugi Kenshin broke through Takeda Shingen's entire army, burst into his command tent on horseback and attacked him with his sword. Shingen deflected the blow with his war fan. It is not clear whether the fan was a tessen, a dansen uchiwa or some other form of fan. It was quite rare for commanders to fight directly, and especially for a general to defend himself so effectively when taken so off-guard.

literature.text: Matsuo Bashō (1644–1694) is recognized as the greatest master of haiku, which was then called hokku. His poems drew on his firsthand experience of the world around him, often capturing the feeling of a scene in a few simple elements.

Chikamatsu Monzaemon (1653–1725) was a jōruri and kabuki dramatist who became popular at the end of the 17th century. He is also known as Japan's Shakespeare. His rise was tied to the growth of working and middle classes in the new capital of Edo.

In 1592 the Amakusa edition of The Tale of the Heike was printed. It translated the work into the vernacular Japanese of the sixteenth century and was written entirely in romanized Japanese. It belongs to Kirishitan Nanban literature, produced by Jesuit missionaries and Japanese Christian communities.

Chōng Ch'ŏl, a poet of the 16th century, is regarded as having perfected gasa, a Korean verse form. Its lines were parallel, each broken into two four-syllable units. Gasa were commonly sung and were popular among yangban women.
Bashō made the transformation of haikai into a literary genre his life's work. For him, haikai combined comic playfulness and spiritual depth with ascetic practice and involvement in human society.
Bashō wrote Oku no Hosomichi, a travel diary dated 1702 in one account. It is considered "one of the major texts of classical Japanese literature."

The history of gasa is divided into two periods, one marked by the Japanese invasion of 1592–97. Earlier gasa were about 100 lines long and treated female beauty, war and seclusion. Later gasa grew longer, dealing with moral instruction, travel accounts, banishment and personal misfortunes.

From the 17th century onwards, fiction became increasingly popular in Korea and more readily available through book rental schemes. Most stories were didactic, emphasizing correct moral conduct, and almost always had happy endings.

In the late Edo period, Motoori Norinaga, the great reviver of traditional Japanese literature, tried to revive waka as a way of providing "traditional feeling expressed in genuine Japanese way". Waka became an important form to his followers, the Kokugaku scholars.

Most earlier gasa writers were yangban, but the later writers were usually commoners. So the Japanese invasion of 1592–97 marks a shift in both the subjects and the authorship of this Korean verse form.

The priest Keinen accompanied the samurai on the Korean campaign of 1592 and kept a diary, "Korea Day by Day." It described the horror and destruction of the invasions. It was so controversial that it remained unpublished until 1965.

Hiraga Gennai (1728–1780) was a scholar of rangaku and a writer of popular fiction. Sugita Genpaku (1733–1817) translated Kaitai Shinsho (New Book of Anatomy) from a Dutch book, the first full translation from a Western language in Japan.

science.text: Japan's isolationist sakoku policy of 1639 spanned the Edo period. Even so, the study of Western sciences, known as rangaku, continued through contact with the Dutch enclave in Nagasaki.

After the Later Jin invasion of 1627 and the Qing invasions of 1636–1637, Joseon experienced a nearly 200-year period of peace and prosperity. It was accompanied by cultural and technological development, even as the kingdom followed an increasingly isolationist policy.
Japan's early study of western science, known as Rangaku, took place during the Edo period (1603–1868). It is described as having partly aided the country's later rapid modernization.

Traditional Japanese time divided daytime and nighttime into six periods each, so their lengths changed with the seasons. European clocks told equal hours that did not vary. Japanese clockmakers showed considerable ingenuity in adapting the European technology to this system, and Tsuda Sukezaemon is reported to have made a mechanical clock in 1598.

Pedro Gómez's Compendium Catholicae Veritatis, written in 1593 and translated into Japanese by 1595, covered Aristotelian cosmology in a section called De Sphaera. It also addressed the philosophy of the soul and post-Tridentine theology.
science.source_title: History of the Catholic Church in Japan

politics.text: Joseon was founded by Taejo in 1392 and lasted 505 years, until it was replaced by the Korean Empire in 1897. Neo-Confucianism was installed as the state's ideology, and Buddhism was discouraged and occasionally persecuted.

Between 1592 and 1598, Japan under Toyotomi Hideyoshi launched invasions of Korea. The advance was halted by Korean forces, righteous army militias formed by civilians, and Ming dynasty Chinese troops, and the Japanese were eventually forced to withdraw.

Beginning in 1587, imperial regent Toyotomi Hideyoshi banned Jesuit missionaries, treating Christianity as a threat to national unity. Under Hideyoshi and the Tokugawa shogunate that followed, Catholic Christianity was repressed and its adherents were persecuted. After the Tokugawa shogunate banned Christianity in 1620, it ceased to exist publicly; many Catholics went underground as hidden Christians, and others lost their lives.

In the 16th century, Portuguese traders and Jesuit missionaries reached Japan and began direct commercial and cultural exchange with the West. Oda Nobunaga used European technology and firearms to conquer many other daimyō. His consolidation of power began the Azuchi–Momoyama period.

The Japanese invasions left the Korean Peninsula devastated, and relations between Korea and Japan were completely suspended until 1609. Joseon and Ming forces had defeated the Japanese, but at a deep price.

Joseon was weakened by the Japanese wars, and the Manchus took advantage by invading in 1627 and 1637. After relations with the Qing dynasty were normalized, Joseon enjoyed a nearly 200-year period of peace.

In 1633, the shogun issued the Sakoku Ordinance to the Nagasaki bugyō, prohibiting people from immigrating to Southeast Asia and ordering expatriate Japanese to move back to Japan. It was issued out of fear of international conflict, and as travel was cut off, Japanese influence abroad diminished.

Gwanghaegun of Joseon, who reigned from 1608 to 1623, tried to stay neutral as Nurhaci and the Ming fought. Nurhaci demanded his help while the Ming court also requested assistance. Most of his officials opposed him for not supporting Ming China, which had saved Joseon during Hideyoshi's invasions.

After the climactic Battle of Sekigahara, ronin migrating out of Japan to Southeast Asia peaked. The Kingdom of Ayutthaya, losing wars against the Burmese Toungoo Empire, hired Japanese mercenaries after Portuguese gun corps hesitated because Toungoo had also hired a Portuguese corps.

From 1670 to 1671, Korea endured a devastating famine brought on by cold weather and poor harvests. The death toll is difficult to measure, but hundreds of thousands of Koreans may have died. Scholars estimate that the Kyŏngsin Famine and the Eulbyeong famine of 1695 to 1696 together may have killed 23 to 33 percent of Korea's population, and the countryside stayed scarred, with population growth depressed for most of the 18th century.

In 1666, during Hyeonjong's reign, the Dutchman Hendrick Hamel left Korea after more than thirteen years of captivity. Joseon's increasingly harsh isolationist policy earned it the name "hermit kingdom" in Western literature.

philosophy.text: Neo-Confucianism was adopted by the 17th-century Tokugawa shogunate as the principle for controlling people. Thinkers such as Hayashi Razan and Arai Hakuseki helped shape Japan's dominant early modern political philosophy.
In Joseon Korea, Neo-Confucianism was epitomized by the seonbi class. These were nobles who passed up positions of wealth and power to lead lives of study and integrity.

Three main Neo-Confucian traditions developed in Japan. Shushigaku followed Zhu Xi and became the cornerstone of education, while Ōyōmeigaku followed Wang Yangming, who held self-knowledge to be the highest form of learning. The Kogaku school tried to revive the original thought of Confucius and Mencius.

The Kokugaku school challenged Neo-Confucianism in the 17th and 18th centuries. Its advocates argued that the ancient Japanese were better representatives of Confucian virtues than the ancient Chinese, and urged more focus on Japanese classics and Shinto.

In Korea, Silhak (Practical Learning) scholars were attracted to Catholic doctrines that reached Korea through the writings of Matteo Ricci. A study of 1801 found that more than half of the families that had converted to Catholicism were linked to the Silhak school.

Jesuit colleges in Funai and Amakusa introduced a curriculum that blended European liberal arts with Japanese language and culture. They were led by figures like Pedro Gómez, who served as Vice-Provincial from 1590 to 1600.
philosophy.source_title: History of the Catholic Church in Japan

philosophy.text: The Jesuit Pedro Gómez wrote the Compendium Catholicae Veritatis in 1593, and it was translated into Japanese by 1595. It covered Aristotelian cosmology, philosophy of the soul, and post-Tridentine theology, and was used in Jesuit colleges at Funai and Amakusa.
philosophy.source_title: History of the Catholic Church in Japan

philosophy.text: In 1614 a statement drafted by the Zen monk Konchiin Suden was issued in the name of shōgun Hidetada, ordering the expulsion of all missionaries. It claimed Christians were bringing disorder to Japanese society and that they traduced Shinto and calumniated the True Law.
philosophy.source_title: History of the Catholic Church in Japan

philosophy.text: Largely because converts refused to perform Confucian ancestral rituals, the Joseon government prohibited the proselytisation of Christianity. Some Catholics were executed during the early 19th century, though the restrictive law was not strictly enforced. Yi Sung-hun, the first baptised Korean, had returned from Beijing about a decade before the first Catholic missionaries arrived in 1794.

culture.text: In 16th-century Japan, the art of the tea ceremony was formalized. Tea later spread beyond the elite during the Edo period, when it became a popular beverage consumed by all strata of society. New ways of preparing it appeared, starting with sencha, a steamed brew that became the most common.

Japanese Christianity began in 1549, when the Jesuits Francis Xavier, Cosme de Torres and Juan Fernández landed in Kagoshima on 15 August. Portuguese traders had been active there since 1543 and were welcomed by local daimyōs because they imported gunpowder. A Japanese convert named Anjirō helped the Jesuits understand Japanese culture and translated the first Japanese catechism.

Japan's invasion of Korea in 1592 helped spark dramatic change in Japanese printing, alongside the Jesuit press set up in Kyushu in 1590. Hideyoshi and his generals used the war to loot valuable commodities from Korea and to kidnap skilled Korean craftsmen and take them back to Japan. Korean books and metal movable type were top priorities for looting, and one commander, Ukita Hideie, is said to have had 200,000 printing types and books removed from Gyeongbokgung Palace. Before 1590, Buddhist monasteries handled virtually all book printing in Japan.

Sen no Rikyū (1522–1591) was the leading figure in the development of the Japanese tea ceremony. Although he was the son of a Sakai fishmonger, he studied tea with Takeno Jōō and served as tea master to Oda Nobunaga and Toyotomi Hideyoshi. In 1591, Hideyoshi forced him to commit suicide, but allowed his descendants and disciples to carry on his role as tea master.

Under Hideyoshi and the Tokugawa shogunate, Catholic Christianity was repressed and its adherents persecuted. During Toyotomi rule especially, foreign missionaries were killed in Japan, some by Japanese-style crucifixion. In 1597 the twenty-six martyrs of Japan were tortured and crucified on crosses outside Nagasaki to discourage Christianity, and there were further persecutions and martyrdoms in 1613, 1622, 1623, 1630, 1632 and 1634.

Confucianism was introduced to Japan from Korea during the Japanese invasions of Korea (1592–1598). It developed into an elite religion, yet had a profound influence on the fabric of Japanese society during the Edo period. Its rationalism stood in contrast to the mysticism of Zen Buddhism.

Mechanical clocks reached Japan in the 16th century through Jesuit missionaries. Francis Xavier gave one to the daimyō Ouchi Yoshitaka in 1551, and Tokugawa Ieyasu received two clocks, in 1606 and 1611. The oldest surviving Western clock in Japan dates to 1612, a gift to Ieyasu from the viceroy of Mexico.

The tea ceremony style was marked by whipped tea and a meal called kaiseki. It incorporated wabi, the pursuit of elegance in simplicity and tranquility, and sabi, a nostalgic contemplation of the passage of time that valued aged, rustic objects. After Rikyū's departure, the ritual split into several schools, each led by a master called an iemoto.

The Tokugawa shoguns eradicated Christianity in Japan through murder, persecution and decrees. After the Shimabara Rebellion of 1638, where an estimated 37,000 people, mostly Christians, were massacred, the remaining Christians were forced to publicly renounce their faith. Catholicism went underground, its rites preserved by the Kakure Kirishitan, or hidden Christians, who kept practicing in secret private devotion.

In 1593 a Korean printing press with movable type was sent as a present for Emperor Go-Yōzei. He commanded that it be used to print an edition of the Confucian Classic of Filial Piety. In 1599, a Japanese version of the press, built with wooden type in 1597, printed the first part of the Nihon Shoki.
Eighty percent of Japan's book production was printed using moveable type between 1593 and 1625. Ultimately, though, woodblock printing supplanted moveable type, which was rarely used after 1650.
